question_text: Examine the pattern and trend of public expenditure on social services in the post-reforms period in India. To what extent has this been in consonance with the objective of inclusive growth?
customKeyPointers: Social spending rose in rupees and stayed modest as a share
Health and education grew slower than the need
Inclusion needs the spend to reach the last person, not only the budget line

points.text: After the reforms, India spent more on social services in absolute terms, and not enough to match the claim of inclusive growth.
Education and health rose, with a later push on a rural guarantee, a food law and a health cover. As a share of GDP the rise was uneven and often stalled.
Inclusive growth needed a larger, better-aimed spend. Leakage and a weak local delivery kept part of it from the poorest.
The pattern moved toward inclusion. It has not gone far enough to say the objective has been met.

question_text: What are the causes of persistent high food inflation in India? Comment on the effectiveness of the monetary policy of the RBI to control this type of inflation.
topic: Food inflation and the limits of monetary policy
topics: Food inflation and the limits of monetary policy
customKeyPointers: Food prices rise from a supply shock more often than from too much money
A rate hike cools demand and does not grow a vegetable
Monetary policy is a weak tool for this inflation and a guard against it spreading

points.text: Persistent food inflation in India is mostly a supply problem that a central bank can only partly touch.
Erratic rain, a concentrated market, a thin cold chain and a sudden export or import decision keep vegetable, pulse and cereal prices high for long stretches.
The RBI can raise rates to stop the rise from entering wages and other prices. It cannot produce the onion.
Monetary policy is effective against the second round. It is not an effective cure for the food price itself.

question_text: What were the factors responsible for the successful implementation of land reforms in some parts of the country? Elaborate.
topic: Why land reform worked in some regions
topics: Why land reform worked in some regions
customKeyPointers: Political will at the state level
A peasant movement made concealment costly
Good records and a committed revenue staff made the ceiling real

points.text: Land reform worked where a state government wanted it to, and had a countryside that would not let records be hidden.
A strong tenancy movement, updated land records and officers who were not themselves landlords distinguished those regions.
Where the same law met a hostile local elite and a paper record, the surplus disappeared.
The factors were political will, organisation of the tenant, and an administration that recorded the land as it was.

question_text: Explain the role of millets for ensuring health and nutritional security in India.
customKeyPointers: Millets carry fibre and minerals, and they grow where rice and wheat strain the water
Nutritional security is a diet, not only a calorie
The role depends on people actually eating them

points.text: Millets can improve India's nutrition because they add what a rice-and-wheat plate is short of, and they grow on less water.
Iron, calcium and fibre in millets matter for anaemia and for a diet that is full of calories and poor in quality.
They also suit dryland farmers, so the crop and the meal can be the same household's.
Their role is real if procurement, a public meal and a habit change together. A campaign alone does not feed anyone.

question_text: What is the present world scenario of intellectual property rights with respect to life materials? Although India is second in the world in filing patents, still only a few have been commercialised. Explain the reasons behind this less commercialisation.
topic: Patents on life materials and weak commercialisation
topics: Patents on life materials and weak commercialisation
customKeyPointers: The world is split on whether a gene, a seed or a cell can be owned
India files many patents and sells few
The gap is a missing fund, a missing firm, and a lab that stops at the paper

points.text: On life materials the world is divided between broad patents on a gene or a seed and a resistance, strong in India, to owning life itself.
India now files a large number of patents. Very few become a product, a licence or a firm.
The reasons are a weak link from laboratory to industry, little patient capital, an unused university patent, and a filing made for a metric rather than for a market.
Commercialisation is low because the system rewards the application, not the buyer.

question_text: What is the technology being employed for electronic toll collection on highways? What are its advantages and limitations? What are the proposed changes that will make this process seamless? Would this transition bring any potential threat?
topic: Electronic toll collection and the next change
topics: Electronic toll collection and the next change
customKeyPointers: The present tool is a radio tag deducted at a plaza
It is faster than cash and still stops the vehicle in a queue
A gantry or a satellite charge would not need a stop
The threat is a wrong deduction and a privacy trail

points.text: Highways now collect toll by a radio tag in the vehicle, read at a plaza and deducted from a prepaid account.
The advantage is speed and less cash leakage. The limitation is that a plaza still exists, a tag fails, and a lane becomes a queue.
The proposed change is a barrier-free, distance-based charge using satellite location or a gantry, so the vehicle need not stop.
The threat is an error that is hard to dispute, and a continuous record of where the vehicle went.

question_text: Industrial pollution of river water is a significant environmental issue in India. Discuss the various mitigation measures to deal with this problem and also the government's initiatives in this regard.
customKeyPointers: Treat the waste before discharge and stop the untreated outfall
A common plant works only if the factory is connected and the plant actually runs
The law exists; the inspector and the continuous monitor are the gap

points.text: Industrial pollution of rivers is mitigated by not letting an untreated effluent reach the water.
Zero-liquid aims, a common effluent plant, and a continuous online monitor are the technical measures. A closure notice is the legal one.
Namami Gange and similar basin programmes, consent to operate, and a real-time monitoring network are the government's initiatives.
The initiatives are serious on paper. The river improves only when a non-working plant is actually shut.

question_text: What role do environmental NGOs and activists play in influencing Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) outcomes for major projects in India? Cite four examples with all important details.
customKeyPointers: An NGO can force a study to include the people and the harm it skipped
The tools are a hearing, a court and a public record
Influence is not the same as a veto

points.text: Environmental NGOs and activists change EIA outcomes by supplying the facts a project report leaves out and by taking them to a hearing or a court.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan forced rehabilitation and a long judicial scrutiny of the Sardar Sarovar project. Activists and fishworkers pushed the Kudankulam nuclear plant's clearance into the Supreme Court on safety and livelihood.

Protests and litigation around the Sterlite copper plant in Thoothukudi ended in a closure after years of pollution complaints. Campaigners against the Vedanta bauxite project in the Niyamgiri hills secured a village consent that stopped the mine.
Their role is to make an assessment answer the people it affects. They influence the outcome. They do not replace the authority that clears it.

question_text: Explain how narco-terrorism has emerged as a serious threat across the country. Suggest suitable measures to counter narco-terrorism.
customKeyPointers: The drug trade funds the gun, and the gun protects the drug
The route runs from a border drop to a city market
The counter is the route, the money and the demand together

points.text: Narco-terrorism is the use of a drug trade to finance and arm terror, and of terror to protect that trade.
Drones, a sea route and a corrupt local link have spread it from the border districts into the hinterland.
The measures are a tighter watch on the drop, a pursuit of the money, a faster case, and a reduction of demand so the market shrinks.
Treating the drug and the terror as two files is how the threat grew. They have to be worked as one.

question_text: Describe the context and salient features of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
topic: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
topics: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
customKeyPointers: A digital state and a digital market hold everyone's data
Consent, a purpose limit and a penalty are the core
The state keeps wide exceptions, which is the Act's tension

points.text: The 2023 Act was passed because identity, payments and private platforms had come to hold personal data with no single law governing it.
It requires consent for a stated purpose, lets the person correct or erase data, and sets a duty on the body that decides the purpose.
A board can penalise a breach. The state may process data for specified public uses with fewer of those duties.
The salient feature is a consent-based right. The salient limit is how wide the state's own use remains.

question_text: Discuss the merits and demerits of the four Labour Codes in the context of labour market reforms in India. What has been the progress so far in this regard?
customKeyPointers: Four codes replaced a thicket of laws
The merit is one definition, one return and easier compliance
The demerit is thinner protection and a slow, uneven start

points.text: The four Labour Codes on wages, industrial relations, social security and safety were meant to turn many old Acts into one readable set.
The merits are a common definition of a worker, a single registration and return, a wider promise of social security, and a threshold that lets a smaller firm adjust its staff.
The demerits are a higher bar for a strike, a weaker inspection in some readings, and a fear that ease for the firm is a loss for the worker who was already informal.
The codes are enacted. Many rules are notified unevenly across states, and the old practice has not yet been fully replaced.
The reform is real on the statute book and incomplete on the shop floor.

question_text: What is the need for expanding regional air connectivity in India? In this context, discuss the government's UDAN scheme and its achievements.
customKeyPointers: A large country cannot move only through a few metros
UDAN subsidises a seat so a thin route can start
A route often stops when the subsidy does

points.text: India needs regional air links because rail and road leave many district towns a full day away from a city that has the service they need.
UDAN offers a viability support and a capped fare so an airline will fly a route that would not pay on its own, and it has revived unused airstrips.
The achievement is a large number of routes and a first flight for towns that had none. Some routes have found steady passengers.
Others closed when the support ended, and slots, a small aircraft and a trained crew remain scarce.
The need is clear and the scheme has opened the map. A route that survives without the subsidy is the achievement that still has to be proved.

question_text: What are the major challenges faced by the Indian irrigation system in recent times? State the measures taken by the government for efficient irrigation management.
customKeyPointers: The canal does not reach, and the well is overdrawn
Water is lost between the dam and the field
The measures are micro-irrigation, a piped canal and a local user group

points.text: Indian irrigation is challenged by a gap between the water that is stored and the water that reaches a root.
Aging canals, a tail-end that stays dry, falling groundwater, and a crop choice that drinks more than the region has, are the present problems. A changing rain makes them worse.
The government has pushed micro-irrigation, piped distribution, participatory management by water users, and a faster completion of pending projects.
Efficiency also needs a price and a crop pattern that do not reward the most wasteful use.
The measures are aimed at the right loss. They work where the last mile is actually built and maintained.

question_text: Elucidate the importance of buffer stocks for stabilizing agricultural prices in India. What are the challenges associated with the storage of buffer stocks? Discuss.
topic: Buffer stocks and the problem of storing them
topics: Buffer stocks and the problem of storing them
customKeyPointers: A buffer releases stock in a shortage and buys in a glut
Storage is the hard part: quantity, quality and cost
A stock that rots is a stabiliser that failed

points.text: A buffer stock lets the state buy when the harvest crashes the price and sell when a shortage would spike it.
That is its importance for wheat and rice in particular: a minimum price for the farmer and a ration for the consumer from the same pile.
The challenges are godowns that are full or unfit, moisture and pests, a high carrying cost, and a stock so large that it distorts the market it was meant to steady.
A decentralised storage, a modern silo and a rule for when to release would keep the buffer from becoming a permanent pile.
The buffer is important. Its storage is the point at which the policy either works or wastes the grain.

question_text: The world is facing an acute shortage of clean and safe freshwater. What are the alternative technologies which can solve this crisis? Briefly discuss any three such technologies, citing their key merits and demerits.
topic: Three technologies for the freshwater crisis
topics: Three technologies for the freshwater crisis
customKeyPointers: Desalination, reuse of wastewater and rain harvesting
Each shifts a cost: energy, trust or storage
None replaces a decision to use less

points.text: Alternative technologies can add or recover freshwater. They do not abolish the shortage by themselves.
Desalination turns sea water into drinking water. Its merit is a source that does not depend on rain. Its demerit is the energy and the brine.
Treated wastewater can be reused for industry and, with a higher treatment, for drinking. The merit is a second use of a city effluent. The demerit is cost and public distrust.
Rainwater harvesting stores a local fall. The merit is simplicity. The demerit is that a failed monsoon leaves the tank empty, and a dirty roof spoils it.
The three help in different places. A technology is a supplement to using the water one already has more carefully.

question_text: What are asteroids? How real is the threat of them causing extinction of life? What strategies have been developed to prevent such a catastrophe?
customKeyPointers: An asteroid is a rocky body left from the making of the planets
A civilisation-ending strike is rare and not imaginary
The strategy is to find it early and nudge it
A late discovery leaves only evacuation

points.text: Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies, mostly in a belt between Mars and Jupiter, that are leftovers of the early solar system.
A large impact can cause a mass extinction, as one is believed to have done for the dinosaurs. The chance in any given century is very small, and the consequence is large enough to plan for.
The strategy is a survey that finds a threatening object years ahead, and a deflection: a kinetic impact, demonstrated by NASA's DART mission, that changes its speed enough to miss the Earth.
A nuclear option is discussed only for a late, large object. Evacuation is the last resort for a small, local hit.
The threat is real and infrequent. The useful strategy is early discovery and a small push, not a last-minute drama.

question_text: What is disaster resilience? How is it determined? Describe various elements of a resilience framework. Also mention the global targets of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030).
topic: Disaster resilience and the Sendai targets
topics: Disaster resilience and the Sendai targets
customKeyPointers: Resilience is the ability to absorb a disaster and recover without permanent loss
A framework joins a warning, a building, a livelihood and a government
Sendai aims at fewer deaths, fewer people affected, and less economic loss

points.text: Disaster resilience is the capacity of a people and a place to withstand a hazard, respond, and recover to at least the life they had.
It is determined by the hazard, the exposure, the vulnerability, and the capacity to warn, shelter and rebuild.
A framework includes a risk assessment, an early warning, a resistant infrastructure, a prepared community, a social protection for the poorest, and a government that can coordinate.

The Sendai Framework's global targets to 2030 are to cut deaths, the number of affected people, economic loss and damage to infrastructure, to increase the number of countries with a strategy, to improve international cooperation, and to increase access to a multi-hazard warning.
Resilience is not the absence of the disaster. It is a measured reduction of what the disaster is allowed to destroy.

question_text: Flooding in urban areas is an emerging climate-induced disaster. Discuss the causes of this disaster. Mention the features of two major floods in the last two decades in India. Describe the policies and frameworks in India that aim at tackling such floods.
customKeyPointers: A hotter climate gives a heavier short rain
A paved city gives that rain nowhere to go
The policy exists and the drain often does not

points.text: Urban flooding is now a climate disaster because a heavier cloudburst meets a city that has paved over its own drainage.
The causes are intense rain, a lost lake and wetland, a choked drain, an encroached floodplain and a storm water system built for a gentler past.

The 2015 Chennai floods drowned a city whose tanks and the Adyar floodplain had been built over. The 2005 Mumbai floods showed a century-old drain and a high tide meeting one day's extreme rain. Kerala in 2018 showed the same water overwhelming a dense urban stretch.
The National Disaster Management guidelines on urban flooding, a city disaster plan, and programmes to restore a water body are the frameworks.
The policy names the problem. Tackling it means giving the water a path the city has spent fifty years closing.

question_text: India has a long and troubled border with China and Pakistan, fraught with contentious issues. Examine the conflicting issues and security challenges along the border. Also give out the development works being undertaken under the Border Area Development Programme (BADP) and the Border Infrastructure and Management (BIM) Scheme.
topic: The China and Pakistan borders and border development
topics: The China and Pakistan borders and border development
subTopics: India's borders with China and Pakistan
customKeyPointers: The conflicts are territory, a line that is not agreed, and the use of proxy force
The ground is high, long and thinly held
Development means a road, a fence and a civilian life in the border district

points.text: India's borders with China and Pakistan are unsettled lines along which a territorial dispute and a security problem are the same geography.

With Pakistan the issues are Kashmir, a ceasefire line that is also a launch pad for infiltration, and a drone and a tunnel. With China they are an undemarcated Line of Actual Control, a build-up in Ladakh and a refusal to accept the status of Arunachal.
The challenge is distance, weather and a neighbour who can change facts on the ground faster than a road can be built.

BADP funds schools, a health post and a livelihood in the border block so that people stay. The Border Infrastructure and Management scheme funds a road, a fence, a floodlight and a battalion post so that the force can.
Development and management are the two ways of holding a border that diplomacy has not yet settled.

question_text: Social media and encrypting messaging services pose a serious security challenge. What measures have been adopted at various levels to address the security implications of social media? Also suggest any other remedies to address the problem.
customKeyPointers: The challenge is speed, anonymity and a message the state cannot read
Encryption protects a citizen and hides a crime
The remedy is lawful, targeted access, not a back door for everyone

points.text: Social media spreads a harm in minutes, and an encrypted message can hide the planning of it from everyone but the two ends.
India has used the IT Act and its intermediary rules to demand a grievance officer, a takedown and a trace of a first originator in defined cases. Police units now monitor open platforms.
Platforms have their own reporting and a label on a forwarded message. None of this opens a fully encrypted chat without breaking the encryption for all users.
Further remedies are a faster lawful process for a specific account, a better digital literacy, and a refusal of a general back door that would make every citizen's message less safe.
